conclusion.justification: The report concludes that hypnosis has not been shown reliably to improve long-term smoking cessation, citing evidence that it does not perform better than other support or quitting without assistance. Therefore, it considers the claim unsupported and rejects it.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
## Conclusion

**Hypnosis/hypnotherapy has not been shown reliably to improve long-term smoking cessation.** The best available review evidence finds insufficient evidence that it works better than other behavioral support or quitting without assistance; if there is a benefit, it is likely small. Individual studies vary substantially in methods and quality, so hypnosis should not replace proven cessation treatment.

A NICE evidence review similarly reports meta-analysis evidence that hypnotherapy does **not** improve long-term quitting outcomes.

If someone finds hypnosis motivating or relaxing, it may be reasonable as an *adjunct* to a structured quit plan—but it should be paired with evidence-based care. For nonpregnant adults, recommended treatments include behavioral counseling and FDA-approved medications; using counseling and medication together offers the best chance of quitting.

**Sources**

- Cochrane review (full text): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6568235/  
- NICE evidence review: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng209/evidence/ph10-rapid-review-of-nonnhs-treatments-for-smoking-cessation-pdf-392073181532  
- U.S. Preventive Services Task Force: https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/tobacco-use-in-adults-and-pregnant-women-counseling-and-interventions  
- CDC, quitting smoking: https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco/about/how-to-quit.html
